Sridhar Vembu says Raghuram Rajan’s ‘Chicago School’ economics can make India like Mexico

The clash between Sridhar Vembu and Raghuram Rajan centres on a fundamental disagreement over how India should build wealth and elevate its workforce to high-paying jobs.

Sagrika Kissu

04 September, 2026 05:14 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of former RBI governor Raghuram Rajan and Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu | Source: Bloomberg, Facebook

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Zoho founder and chief scientist Sridhar Vembu took a swipe at former RBI governor Raghuram Rajan, saying that India cannot complain about low-paying factory jobs while shunning the industrial policy.

In an interview on September 1, Rajan questioned India’s push to develop the domestic semiconductor industry. He said that most chipsets are “the most easily smuggled thing on Earth,” with China and Russia already smuggling them en masse. Rajan further questioned the “effectiveness of the government’s broader industrial policy of picking sectors for targeted support.”

He further presented Tamil Nadu as an example.

Show Full Article

“What kind of manufacturing jobs are you getting? They pay in the enterprises that assemble products and all that is not different from the pay the driver gets or a house help gets in Chennai. It’s Rs 20,000 per month. It’s not that great. We need to figure out how we can get better jobs.”

In his response, Vembu wrote a long post on X. His main argument centred on India’s economic model that relies heavily on exporting services while failing to build and own intellectual property (IP).

“High paying jobs, which I agree we need, come from high value addition and that requires that we not only perform the R&D but we also own the IP in India and capture the resulting economic value addition. Only then would pay in even products where India does not have much IP (like the iPhone) would go up,” Vembu wrote on X.

Also read: American prisoners are now calling voters to campaign for Republican candidates

Vembu’s developmental model of India Vembu went on to illustrate with what he called two “crude examples”. His first example is Nvidia and its gross profit of more than $200 billion a year.

“…And 24 per cent of Nvidia employees are in India, mostly in R&D. Microsoft has a gross profit of about $230 billion a year and 10 per cent of its R&D staff are in India. India’s economic accounts will not show anywhere near 24 per cent of value added by Nvidia or 10 per cent of value added by Microsoft,” Vembu wrote on X. “If we look at major IP-rich, successful companies in the world, all of them do substantial R&D in India. But only a tiny fraction of economic value added by these companies actually is accounted for in India.”

His central argument revolved around what development model India should follow to become a developed economy.

“The only mechanism the world has known for a “developing country” (no IP, low value addition) to become a “developed country” (lots of IP and value addition captured locally) is to spur the domestic entrepreneurs and industry to gain the know-how and capability,” he added on X.

Vembu termed Rajan’s arguments as inspired by the “Chicago School” of economic theory. The Chicago School, he says, does not agree with industrial policy.

And then he says that such a school of economic theory would lead us to Mexico’s economic situation but never to Japan or Taiwan or South Korea and now, China.

“Getting to Japan or Taiwan or South Korea or China requires us to understand “How Asia Works.” China rose from very low wages and now has overtaken nations like Mexico, because China has the know-how and IP and Mexico does not.”

(Edited by Saptak Datta)

JD Vance joke on journalists sparks backlash. ‘Nice reporters’ or ‘missed their coffee’?

The comment comes as Vance faces heightened scrutiny over the US-Iran conflict and reports of civilian deaths in a recent airstrike in Iran.

Saman Husain

04 September, 2026 02:39 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of US Vice President JD Vance | Jonathan Ernst | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: US Vice President JD Vance has drawn criticism online after joking that he would find out which reporters were “going to be nice” before entering the White House press briefing room.

In a video shared by Vance on Instagram, he was seen heading to the briefing room to take questions from reporters. On his way in, he joked: “We’re going to find out which reporters are going to be nice and which missed their cups of coffee.”

The remark triggered a sharply divided response on social media, with supporters praising Vance for confronting what they described as a hostile media, while critics accused him of treating journalists as adversaries rather than recognising their role in holding public officials accountable.

Show Full Article

One commenter said answering difficult questions was part of Vance’s job because he worked for US taxpayers, adding that he and President Donald Trump had “forgotten” that they were public servants.

Others defended the vice president, with one commenter saying they were pleased to see Vance “actually able to speak with integrity to the fake news media”.

Also Read: ‘Call Bobby Kennedy’: JD Vance reveals his weight-loss secret

Vance faces questions over Iran The backlash comes amid heightened scrutiny of Vance and the Trump administration’s handling of the ongoing US-Iran conflict.

Vance has recently faced reporters over the administration’s military actions against Iran, including reports that a US airstrike in southern Iran struck a wedding gathering and killed civilians.

Washington has said it does not target civilians and is investigating the reports. However, Iranian officials have said five people were killed and nearly 70 were wounded in the strike in Kuhestak village in Sirik County.

Vance has also rejected describing the confrontation with Iran as a war, saying the US had ended major combat operations and was focused on preventing Tehran from disrupting commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Edited by Maryam Hassan

‘Call Bobby Kennedy’: JD Vance reveals his weight-loss secret

The vice president made the remarks during a White House press briefing on Thursday, where he also faced questions about Iran.

Almina Khatoon

04 September, 2026 01:20 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

US Vice President JD Vance | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: US Vice President JD Vance revealed that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. played a role in his weight-loss journey, joking that Kennedy’s strict health advice helped him shed the pounds.

Vance made the remarks during a White House press briefing on Thursday, when reporters asked him about his weight loss.

“So, when you’re the vice president of the United States and one of the first questions at a press conference in the White House is how much weight you’ve lost, you must have gotten very fat,” Vance joked in response to the questions.

Show Full Article

Vance said Kennedy, whom he described as being “really into health,” influenced his decision to begin his weight-loss journey around Lent in February. He said he had called Kennedy and told him he was considering giving up sugar.

“Bobby Kennedy says, ‘No, no, no, no, I’ve got something that’s way better than that and way more intense.’ And basically … I eat a lot of high-protein stuff, and I eat a lot of sauerkraut. And let’s just say that if that was Fat Tuesday, Fat Wednesday never came,” Vance said.

Taking a lighthearted approach to the question, Vance further joked about Kennedy’s strict health advice and going to him if anybody needs health advice.

“So, my advice to you is that if you want to lose weight, call Bobby Kennedy. And if you want to enjoy what you eat, do not call Bobby Kennedy,” he said.

Vance on US-Iran conflict The weight-loss exchange came during the first White House press briefing in more than 40 days, following the departure of former press secretary Karoline Leavitt at the end of August.

Reporters also questioned Vance about the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, including recent strikes.

“I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now there’s no active shooting. I recognize there have been places where this has flared up,” Vance said.

He said major combat operations were not currently taking place.

“Major combat operations are currently not ongoing, and they haven’t been ongoing in a very long time,” he said.

Vance was also asked about Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s prediction in July that gas prices could fall to $3 a gallon by Labor Day. Vance said Bessent had only suggested that this “maybe” could happen because energy prices can be difficult to predict.

“I’m not going to make a promise about when it’s going to return to $3,” Vance said, responding to reporters
